blocks.en: Is Faith the Enemy of Science?
blocks.es_reference: ¿Es la Fe Enemiga de la Ciencia?

blocks.en: A young believer is often told, with great confidence, that he must choose: either he can be a thinking person who trusts science, or he can be a Christian, but he cannot be both. The two are said to be at war, and faith is expected to surrender. I want to take that charge head on, and I want to begin by saying something that may surprise you: I love science, and so should you. The study of the natural world is one of the noblest things a human mind can do, and the Christian has every reason to honor it. Indeed, many of the founders of modern science — Kepler, Boyle, Newton among them — were believing men who expected the universe to be orderly precisely because they believed a reasonable God had made it, and historians of science recognize that theological conviction as a real motivating force in the Scientific Revolution, even though the full story of how modern science arose is historically complex and draws on many streams, including the mathematics and astronomy of earlier Greek, Islamic, and other civilizations. The quarrel is not between faith and science. The quarrel is between faith and a philosophy that has dressed itself in a lab coat and hopes you will not notice the difference.
blocks.es_reference: A un joven creyente a menudo se le dice, con gran seguridad, que debe escoger: o puede ser una persona pensante que confía en la ciencia, o puede ser cristiano, pero no puede ser ambas cosas. Se dice que las dos están en guerra, y se espera que la fe se rinda. Quiero enfrentar esa acusación de frente, y quiero comenzar diciendo algo que tal vez le sorprenda: yo amo la ciencia, y usted también debería. El estudio del mundo natural es una de las cosas más nobles que una mente humana puede hacer, y el cristiano tiene toda razón para honrarlo. De hecho, muchos de los fundadores de la ciencia moderna — Kepler, Boyle, Newton entre ellos — fueron hombres creyentes que esperaban que el universo fuera ordenado precisamente porque creían que un Dios razonable lo había hecho, y los historiadores de la ciencia reconocen esa convicción teológica como una fuerza motivadora real en la Revolución Científica, aunque la historia completa de cómo surgió la ciencia moderna es históricamente compleja y bebe de muchas corrientes, incluyendo las matemáticas y la astronomía de civilizaciones griegas, islámicas y otras anteriores. La disputa no es entre la fe y la ciencia. La disputa es entre la fe y una filosofía que se ha vestido con una bata de laboratorio y espera que usted no note la diferencia.

blocks.en: The How and the Why
blocks.es_reference: El Cómo y el Porqué

blocks.en: To see the trick, you must learn to separate two different kinds of questions that are forever being run together. Science is magnificent at investigating mechanisms and causes within nature — how a star burns, why a cell divides the way it does, why an illness spreads through a population. To these the laboratory speaks with marvelous authority, and we are all in its debt; science can and does investigate many causal "why" questions of this kind. But there is a different kind of question — the question of ultimate purpose, meaning, or value — and here empirical investigation, by its very method, cannot settle the matter one way or the other. Why is there a universe rather than nothing? Why is it lawful and beautiful instead of mere chaos? Why am I here, and what am I for? Consider a kettle boiling on the stove. A scientist can tell you, with perfect accuracy, that the water boils because heat is agitating the molecules until they escape as steam. That is a true causal explanation. But it is not the whole truth, for there is also a further question of purpose: the water is boiling because I want a cup of tea. The two answers do not compete; they belong to different orders. The man who insists that the molecules are the only real explanation, and that the tea is a fairy tale, has not been more scientific. He has merely gone deaf to half of reality.
blocks.es_reference: Para ver el truco, debe aprender a separar dos clases distintas de preguntas que constantemente se confunden. La ciencia es magnífica para investigar mecanismos y causas dentro de la naturaleza — cómo arde una estrella, por qué se divide una célula de cierta manera, por qué se propaga una enfermedad en una población. A estas el laboratorio habla con maravillosa autoridad, y todos estamos en deuda con él; la ciencia puede investigar, y de hecho investiga, muchas preguntas causales de "por qué" de este tipo. Pero hay una clase distinta de pregunta — la pregunta del propósito último, el significado o el valor — y aquí la investigación empírica, por su propio método, no puede resolver el asunto en un sentido u otro. ¿Por qué hay un universo en lugar de nada? ¿Por qué es ordenado y hermoso en lugar de puro caos? ¿Por qué estoy yo aquí, y para qué? Considere una tetera hirviendo en la estufa. Un científico puede decirle, con perfecta exactitud, que el agua hierve porque el calor agita las moléculas hasta que escapan como vapor. Esa es una verdadera explicación causal. Pero no es toda la verdad, pues hay también una pregunta adicional de propósito: el agua hierve porque yo quiero una taza de té. Las dos respuestas no compiten; pertenecen a órdenes distintos. El hombre que insiste en que las moléculas son la única explicación real, y que el té es un cuento de hadas, no ha sido más científico. Solo se ha vuelto sordo a la mitad de la realidad.

blocks.en: The Naked Ape
blocks.es_reference: El Mono Desnudo

blocks.en: Here is where the philosophy overreaches. It tells you that you are nothing but a naked ape, nothing but a robot built by your genes, nothing but a chance arrangement of atoms briefly holding together before it scatters. Notice that little word, nothing but; it is the most dishonest phrase in the whole debate. It is quite true that a man is, among other things, a remarkable animal, and that he is made of atoms obeying the laws of chemistry. The Christian need not flinch at any of that. But the leap from "a man is an animal" to "a man is nothing but an animal" is not a finding of science; it is a philosophy smuggled in under the cover of science. Consider a great cathedral. A chemist may analyze it and report, with complete accuracy, that it is nothing but a quantity of limestone and glass. He would be right about the stones and wrong about the cathedral, for he has described everything except the thing that makes it a cathedral. So it is with the man who tells you that love is nothing but chemistry, that thought is nothing but electricity, that you are nothing but an ape. He has weighed the stones and missed the building.
blocks.es_reference: Aquí es donde la filosofía se excede. Le dice que usted no es más que un mono desnudo, no es más que un robot construido por sus genes, no es más que un arreglo casual de átomos que se sostiene brevemente antes de dispersarse. Note esa pequeña frase, no es más que; es la frase más deshonesta de todo el debate. Es muy cierto que un hombre es, entre otras cosas, un animal notable, y que está hecho de átomos que obedecen las leyes de la química. El cristiano no necesita estremecerse ante nada de eso. Pero el salto de "un hombre es un animal" a "un hombre no es más que un animal" no es un hallazgo de la ciencia; es una filosofía metida de contrabando bajo la cobertura de la ciencia. Considere una gran catedral. Un químico puede analizarla e informar, con completa exactitud, que no es más que una cantidad de piedra caliza y vidrio. Tendría razón sobre las piedras y se equivocaría sobre la catedral, pues ha descrito todo excepto aquello que la hace una catedral. Así es con el hombre que le dice que el amor no es más que química, que el pensamiento no es más que electricidad, que usted no es más que un mono. Ha pesado las piedras y ha pasado por alto el edificio.

blocks.en: Even Evolution Needs the Goldilocks
blocks.es_reference: Aun la Evolución Necesita el Goldilocks

blocks.en: "But surely," says the objector, "evolution has explained away the need for a Creator." Let us be careful and fair. Whatever one concludes about how living things have developed and changed over the ages, set that whole question to one side, for it does not touch the deeper point at all. Suppose, for the sake of argument, that life unfolded by gradual natural processes exactly as the textbooks say. You have still explained nothing about the real mystery, for every one of those processes was running inside a universe that was already, astonishingly, fine-tuned to allow it. Before a single cell could divide or a single creature adapt, the great dials we spoke of in Unit Two had already been set with breathtaking precision: the strength of gravity, the charge of the electron, the rate of cosmic expansion, the strange properties of water and carbon. Evolution, if it occurred, did not set those dials; it played the game on a board already laid out for life. To say "evolution did it" is like saying the game of chess explains the existence of the chessboard. The deepest question is not how the pieces moved, but who built the board, and lit the room, and wrote the rules.
blocks.es_reference: "Pero seguramente", dice el objetor, "la evolución ha eliminado la necesidad de un Creador." Seamos cuidadosos y justos. Sea lo que sea que uno concluya sobre cómo los seres vivos se han desarrollado y cambiado a lo largo de las edades, ponga toda esa cuestión a un lado, pues no toca el punto más profundo en absoluto. Suponga, por amor al argumento, que la vida se desplegó por procesos naturales graduales exactamente como dicen los libros de texto. Usted todavía no ha explicado nada sobre el verdadero misterio, pues cada uno de esos procesos corría dentro de un universo que ya estaba, asombrosamente, afinado para permitirlo. Antes de que una sola célula pudiera dividirse o una sola criatura adaptarse, los grandes diales de los que hablamos en la Unidad Dos ya habían sido ajustados con precisión impresionante: la fuerza de la gravedad, la carga del electrón, la tasa de expansión cósmica, las extrañas propiedades del agua y del carbono. La evolución, si ocurrió, no ajustó esos diales; jugó el juego sobre un tablero ya dispuesto para la vida. Decir "la evolución lo hizo" es como decir que el juego de ajedrez explica la existencia del tablero. La pregunta más profunda no es cómo se movieron las piezas, sino quién construyó el tablero, y encendió la sala, y escribió las reglas.

blocks.en: The Watch on the Heath
blocks.es_reference: El Reloj en el Páramo

blocks.en: 💡 Picture a man walking across an open moor. His foot strikes a stone, and if you ask him how it came to be there, he may reasonably say it had simply lain there forever; the stone demands no explanation. But suppose, a little farther on, his foot strikes a watch. He picks it up and opens the case, and there inside are springs and gears and a balance wheel, every part shaped for a purpose and all of them working together to mark the passing hours. He would never say of the watch what he said of the stone. The intricate fitting of means to an end cries out that somewhere there was a watchmaker, even if the man never sees him, even if the watch is old and worn. Now lift your eyes from the watch to the eye that is reading these words — a living lens, focusing light, adjusting to distance, wired to a brain that turns the light into sight. If a watch on the heath demands a watchmaker, what does the eye demand, and the cell, and the coded library of the DNA that builds them both?
blocks.es_reference: 💡 Imagine a un hombre cruzando un páramo abierto. Su pie golpea una piedra, y si usted le pregunta cómo llegó a estar allí, puede razonablemente decir que simplemente había estado allí desde siempre; la piedra no exige explicación. Pero suponga que, un poco más adelante, su pie golpea un reloj. Lo recoge y abre la caja, y allí dentro hay resortes y engranajes y un volante, cada parte formada para un propósito y todas trabajando juntas para marcar las horas que pasan. Jamás diría del reloj lo que dijo de la piedra. El intrincado ajuste de los medios a un fin clama que en algún lugar hubo un relojero, aunque el hombre nunca lo vea, aunque el reloj sea viejo y gastado. Ahora levante los ojos del reloj al ojo que lee estas palabras — un lente vivo, enfocando la luz, ajustándose a la distancia, conectado a un cerebro que convierte la luz en visión. Si un reloj en el páramo exige un relojero, ¿qué exige el ojo, y la célula, y la biblioteca codificada del ADN que construye a ambos?

blocks.en: The Crack at the Bottom of It All
blocks.es_reference: La Grieta en el Fondo de Todo

blocks.en: But the most serious problem for the philosophy of pure matter is not in the stars or the cell. It is much closer to home; it is in the very thoughts by which the unbeliever argues his case. Follow the logic to its end. If my mind is only matter, only the random clattering of atoms in my skull that natural selection arranged for survival and not for truth, then why should I trust a single conclusion it reaches, including the conclusion that my mind is only matter? A man saws off the branch he is sitting on. The one who says "all thought is merely chemistry" has just made a thought, and is asking you to believe it is true and not merely chemical. He cannot have it both ways. The very act of reasoning, the very act of weighing evidence and calling something true, assumes that the mind is more than meat, that it can reach beyond the firing of nerves to touch what is really so. Reason itself is a witness against the creed that reduces reason to chemistry.
blocks.es_reference: Pero el problema más serio para la filosofía de la pura materia no está en las estrellas ni en la célula. Está mucho más cerca de casa; está en los pensamientos mismos con los que el incrédulo argumenta su caso. Siga la lógica hasta el final. Si mi mente es solo materia, solo el traqueteo aleatorio de átomos en mi cráneo que la selección natural arregló para la supervivencia y no para la verdad, entonces ¿por qué debería confiar en una sola conclusión a la que llega, incluida la conclusión de que mi mente es solo materia? Un hombre sierra la rama sobre la que está sentado. El que dice "todo pensamiento es solo química" acaba de hacer un pensamiento, y le pide a usted que crea que es verdadero y no meramente químico. No puede tenerlo de las dos maneras. El acto mismo de razonar, el acto mismo de sopesar evidencia y llamar verdadero a algo, supone que la mente es más que carne, que puede alcanzar más allá del disparo de los nervios para tocar lo que realmente es. La razón misma es un testigo contra el credo que reduce la razón a química.

blocks.en: The Things That Will Not Reduce
blocks.es_reference: Las Cosas que No Se Reducen

blocks.en: And reason is not alone. There are whole regions of your daily experience that the philosophy of "nothing but" can describe but never explain away. There is the abstract thought that lets you do mathematics about infinities you will never see. There is your unshakable sense that some things are truly right and others truly wrong, not merely useful or unpleasant, but wrong — the moral law we met in Unit Two, which no amount of talk about survival has ever managed to dissolve. There is the strange persistent ache for beauty and for meaning, the homesickness for a country you have never visited. A purely material world has no business producing creatures who weep at music, who feel guilt, who ask what it all means and are not satisfied with "it means nothing." These things are not proof in the way a fingerprint is proof, but they are signposts, and they all point the same direction: that you are not an accident, and that the universe is not a closed box of matter, but the workmanship of a Mind.
blocks.es_reference: Y la razón no está sola. Hay regiones enteras de su experiencia diaria que la filosofía del "no es más que" puede describir pero nunca explicar del todo. Está el pensamiento abstracto que le permite hacer matemáticas sobre infinitos que nunca verá. Está su inquebrantable sentido de que algunas cosas son verdaderamente correctas y otras verdaderamente malas, no meramente útiles o desagradables, sino malas — la ley moral que encontramos en la Unidad Dos, que ninguna cantidad de charla sobre la supervivencia ha logrado jamás disolver. Está el extraño y persistente anhelo de belleza y de significado, la nostalgia por un país que nunca ha visitado. Un mundo puramente material no tiene por qué producir criaturas que lloran ante la música, que sienten culpa, que preguntan qué significa todo y no se conforman con "no significa nada." Estas cosas no son prueba al modo en que una huella digital es prueba, pero son señales, y todas apuntan en la misma dirección: que usted no es un accidente, y que el universo no es una caja cerrada de materia, sino la obra de una Mente.

blocks.en: Is the Mind Only the Brain?
blocks.es_reference: ¿Es la Mente Solamente el Cerebro?

blocks.en: Modern neuroscience shows a powerful connection between the brain and our mental life. Damage to the brain can alter memory, personality, and reasoning. But that is not the same as proving that consciousness is nothing more than brain activity. Charles Murray points to the continuing mystery of consciousness and to unusual reports of terminal or paradoxical lucidity, in which some people with severe dementia unexpectedly regain coherent memory or communication, sometimes near death. Medical researchers have documented such episodes, although their cause is not yet understood. They do not prove that the mind exists independently of the brain or that consciousness survives death; neurological explanations remain possible. Their value for apologetics is more modest. They remind us that the relationship between brain and mind is not fully explained. Science can study the brain with extraordinary success without having demonstrated that the person — consciousness, reason, self-awareness, and moral experience — is merely a collection of brain cells.
blocks.es_reference: La neurociencia moderna muestra una poderosa relación entre el cerebro y nuestra vida mental. El daño cerebral puede alterar la memoria, la personalidad y el razonamiento. Pero eso no equivale a demostrar que la conciencia no es nada más que actividad cerebral. Charles Murray señala el misterio continuo de la conciencia y los informes inusuales de lucidez terminal o paradójica, en los que algunas personas con demencia severa recuperan inesperadamente la memoria coherente o la capacidad de comunicarse, a veces cerca de la muerte. Investigadores médicos han documentado tales episodios, aunque todavía no se comprende su causa. No demuestran que la mente exista independientemente del cerebro ni que la conciencia sobreviva a la muerte; siguen siendo posibles explicaciones neurológicas. Su valor para la apologética es más modesto. Nos recuerdan que la relación entre cerebro y mente no está completamente explicada. La ciencia puede estudiar el cerebro con extraordinario éxito sin haber demostrado que la persona — la conciencia, la razón, la autoconciencia y la experiencia moral — sea meramente una colección de células cerebrales.

blocks.en: The One in Whom It All Holds Together
blocks.es_reference: Aquel en Quien Todo Subsiste

blocks.en: So the Christian gives the universe back its second story. Science reads the lower floor and reads it well: the how, the mechanism, the law. But the law itself points upward, for a law implies a Lawgiver, and an orderly cosmos that the human mind can actually understand implies a Mind behind it kin to our own. Paul says it in a single breath: "in Him all things consist" — He holds them together. The very regularities that the scientist studies are the faithful habits of the God who upholds all things by the word of His power. Faith is not the retreat of a frightened mind from the advance of knowledge; it is the larger room in which the knowledge finally makes sense. The naturalist must believe that everything came from nothing, that order came from chaos, that mind came from mindless matter, and that reason can be trusted though it was built by an unreasoning process. Hold those up to the light and tell me honestly which takes the greater faith. I, for one, do not have enough faith to be an unbeliever.
blocks.es_reference: Así que el cristiano le devuelve al universo su segundo piso. La ciencia lee el piso de abajo y lo lee bien: el cómo, el mecanismo, la ley. Pero la ley misma apunta hacia arriba, pues una ley implica un Legislador, y un cosmos ordenado que la mente humana realmente puede entender implica una Mente detrás de él, pariente de la nuestra. Pablo lo dice en un solo aliento: "todas las cosas en él subsisten" — Él las sostiene juntas. Las regularidades mismas que el científico estudia son los hábitos fieles del Dios que sustenta todas las cosas con la palabra de su poder. La fe no es la retirada de una mente asustada ante el avance del conocimiento; es la sala más amplia en la que el conocimiento al fin tiene sentido. El naturalista debe creer que todo vino de la nada, que el orden vino del caos, que la mente vino de la materia sin mente, y que se puede confiar en la razón aunque fue construida por un proceso sin razón. Ponga eso a la luz y dígame honestamente cuál requiere la mayor fe. Yo, por mi parte, no tengo suficiente fe para ser un incrédulo.

sa.prompt: Explain why the unit says the real quarrel is not between faith and science.
sa.model: The unit insists that the quarrel is not between faith and science at all, but between faith and a philosophy that has dressed itself in a lab coat. True science, the study of how the natural world works, is a noble thing the Christian has every reason to honor; in fact many founders of modern science, men like Kepler, Boyle, and Newton, were believing men who expected the universe to be orderly because a reasonable God had made it, and historians recognize that conviction as a real motivating force, even though the fuller history of science's rise is complex and draws on many earlier civilizations as well. What actually opposes faith is naturalism, the philosophy that nothing exists beyond matter, which is smuggled in under the cover of science and presented as though it were a scientific finding. So the believer need not choose between being a thinking person and being a Christian. He simply learns to tell the difference between the genuine work of science and the philosophy that has borrowed its prestige.

sa.prompt: Explain the difference between the 'how' question and the 'why' question, using the boiling-kettle illustration.
sa.model: The unit separates two different kinds of questions that are forever run together. Science is magnificent at investigating mechanisms and causes within nature: how a star burns, how a cell divides. But empirical investigation, by its method, cannot settle the question of ultimate purpose — why there is a universe at all, or what we are here for. The boiling kettle makes the point. A scientist truly explains how the water boils, that heat agitates the molecules until they escape as steam. Yet that is not the whole truth, for there is also a further question of purpose: the water boils because someone wants a cup of tea. The two answers do not compete; they belong to different orders of explanation. The man who insists the molecules are the only real answer and the tea is a fairy tale has not become more scientific; he has simply gone deaf to half of reality, treating the causal explanation as if it were the whole.

sa.prompt: Explain the 'naked ape' / 'nothing but' problem, using the cathedral illustration.
sa.model: The unit warns about the little phrase nothing but, which it calls the most dishonest phrase in the debate. It is true that a man is an animal made of atoms obeying chemistry, and the Christian need not flinch at that. But the leap from a man is an animal to a man is nothing but an animal, a naked ape, is not science but a philosophy smuggled in under science. The cathedral makes it plain. A chemist may analyze a cathedral and report accurately that it is nothing but limestone and glass. He would be right about the stones and wrong about the cathedral, for he has described everything except the thing that makes it a cathedral. In the same way, to say love is nothing but chemistry or that you are nothing but an ape is to weigh the stones and miss the building entirely.

sa.prompt: Why does the unit argue that evolution, even if true, does not remove the need for a Creator?
sa.model: The unit is careful and fair: set aside the whole question of how living things developed, and suppose life unfolded by gradual natural processes exactly as the textbooks say. Even then you have explained nothing about the real mystery, because every one of those processes ran inside a universe that was already fine-tuned to allow it. Before a single cell could divide, the great dials of Unit Two, the strength of gravity, the charge of the electron, the rate of cosmic expansion, the properties of water and carbon, had already been set with breathtaking precision. Evolution, if it occurred, did not set those dials; it played the game on a board already laid out for life. To say evolution did it is like saying the game of chess explains the existence of the chessboard. The deeper question is not how the pieces moved but who built the board, and that still points to a Creator.

sa.prompt: Explain the watch-on-the-heath illustration and how the unit applies it.
sa.model: A man crossing a heath strikes a stone, and he may reasonably say the stone had simply lain there forever, needing no explanation. But a little farther on his foot strikes a watch, and when he opens it he finds springs and gears and a balance wheel, every part shaped for a purpose and all working together to mark the hours. He would never say of the watch what he said of the stone, because the intricate fitting of means to an end cries out for a watchmaker, even one he never sees. The unit then lifts our eyes from the watch to the human eye, a living lens that focuses light and is wired to a brain that turns light into sight. If a mere watch demands a watchmaker, the far more intricate eye, the cell, and the coded library of DNA demand a Designer all the more. The argument is that apparent design in nature points to a real Designer.

sa.prompt: Explain the unit's deepest objection: that pure materialism undercuts reason itself.
sa.model: The unit says the most serious problem for pure materialism is not in the stars but in the very thoughts by which the unbeliever argues. If my mind is only matter, only atoms clattering in my skull that natural selection arranged for survival and not for truth, then why should I trust any conclusion it reaches, including the conclusion that the mind is only matter? The man who says all thought is merely chemistry has just produced a thought and is asking you to accept it as true rather than merely chemical, which is to saw off the branch he is sitting on. The very act of reasoning, of weighing evidence and calling something true, assumes the mind is more than meat and can reach real truth. So reason itself becomes a witness against the creed that reduces reason to chemistry; materialism undercuts the very tool it uses to argue.

sa.prompt: What things does the unit say a 'nothing but' world can describe but never explain away?
sa.model: The unit names several regions of experience that a purely material world can describe but never explain away. There is abstract thought, which lets us do mathematics about infinities we will never see. There is the moral law from Unit Two, the unshakable sense that some things are truly right and others truly wrong, not merely useful, which talk of survival has never dissolved. And there is the persistent ache for beauty and meaning, a homesickness for a country never visited, which leaves us unsatisfied with the answer that it all means nothing. A purely material world has no business producing creatures who weep at music, who feel guilt, and who refuse to accept meaninglessness. The unit calls these not proofs in the way a fingerprint is proof, but signposts that all point the same direction: that we are not an accident and that the universe is the workmanship of a Mind.

sa.prompt: How does Colossians 1:17 frame the Christian answer about the order science studies?
sa.model: The unit gives the universe back its second story. Science reads the lower floor well, the how, the mechanism, the law, but the law itself points upward, because a law implies a Lawgiver, and an orderly cosmos that the human mind can actually understand implies a Mind behind it kin to our own. Colossians 1:17 says that in Christ all things consist, that is, He holds them together. The very regularities the scientist studies are the faithful habits of the God who upholds all things by the word of His power. So the order of nature is not a brute fact standing alone; it is the dependable working of the One who sustains it. This is why faith is not a retreat from knowledge but the larger room in which the findings of science finally make sense, resting on the Christ in whom all things hold together.

sa.prompt: Why does the unit say the naturalist's creed actually takes more faith than belief in a Creator?
sa.model: The unit ends by turning the charge around. The naturalist must believe a chain of remarkable things: that everything came from nothing, that order arose from chaos, that mind came from mindless matter, and that reason can be trusted even though it was built by an unreasoning process aimed only at survival. Each of these is a large act of faith, and held together they are an enormous one. By contrast, the believer holds that a reasonable God made an orderly world and gave creatures minds able to know it, which actually accounts for the order, the reason, and the meaning that the naturalist must take on blind trust. So when the two views are held up to the light, belief in the Creator is the more reasonable, and the unit ends with the course refrain that the author does not have enough faith to be an unbeliever.

sa.prompt: How would you summarize the unit's overall case about science and the limits of naturalism?
sa.model: The unit's overall case is that science and faith are not enemies, but that naturalism, the philosophy that matter is all there is, has limits it hides. Science investigates mechanisms and causes within nature brilliantly, but empirical method by itself does not settle questions of ultimate purpose or meaning, and the phrase nothing but smuggles a philosophy in under that limit. Evolution, even if true, presupposes a fine-tuned universe it did not create, and apparent design like the eye points to a Designer as a watch points to a watchmaker. Most deeply, pure materialism undercuts reason itself, since a mind that is only matter could not be trusted to reach truth, and it cannot explain abstract thought, the moral law, or the ache for meaning. The Christian answer is that a Mind stands behind the order science studies, in whom all things hold together, so that faith is the larger room in which knowledge makes sense, and belief in the Creator takes less faith than unbelief.
